question_en:
An analyst is evaluating the performance of inventory management across several manufacturing companies. The analyst gathers the following data:

# Selected Items from Financial Statements (RUB millions)

| Company | FY17 Cost of Goods Sold | FY17 Average Inventory Balance | FY18 Cost of Goods Sold | FY18 Average Inventory Balance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| X | 60.0 | 10.0 | 60.4 | 9.5 |
| Y | 55.0 | 11.0 | 55.2 | 10.7 |
| Z | 70.0 | 9.0 | 70.0 | 9.4 |
| Industry Average | 61.7 | 10.0 | 61.9 | 9.9 |

Based on the data, and assuming all companies manufacture the same product, which of the following best describes the improvements in the number of days of inventory (DOH) from the previous year?
option_a: Company X shows the most improvement.
option_b: Company Z shows more improvement than Company Y.
option_c: The industry average shows more improvement than Company Y.
explanation_en: The number of days of inventory (DOH), also referred to as days of inventory on hand, measures the average number of days that it takes a company to sell its inventory. Analysts can use DOH to evaluate a company's inventory management. Shorter DOH indicates greater speed and efficiency in selling inventory. In contrast, longer DOH can lead to inventory obsolescence and extra storage costs. Calculate the changes in DOH between FY18 and FY17: Company X improved the most (by 3.4 days) over the previous year. On average, it took Company X 3.4 fewer days to sell its inventory compared to the prior year. (Choice B) Compared with the previous year, Company Z's DOH increased by 2.1 days while Company Y's DOH decreased by 2.2 days. This means that Company Z's DOH worsened by 2.1 days while Company Y's DOH improved by 2.2 days. (Choice C) Compared with the previous year, the industry's DOH decreased by 1 day while Company Y's DOH decreased by 2.2 days. This means that the industry's DOH improved by only 1 day while Company Y's DOH improved by 2.2 days.

question_en:
An analyst is evaluating the performance of three manufacturers with the following information:

| Company | 20X1 ($ millions) Cost of Goods Sold | Inventory Beginning Balance | Inventory Ending Balance |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | 6.0 | 1.4 | 1.4 |
| Y | 7.3 | 2.2 | 1.8 |
| Z | 5.0 | 1.8 | 1.4 |

Which company has the highest inventory turnover?
explanation_en: The inventory turnover ratio represents the number of times, on average, inventory is sold and replenished during a fiscal period. It is calculated by dividing the cost of goods sold (COGS) by the average inventory. Average inventory is used since inventory fluctuates throughout the year. COGS, or the cost at which the inventory was acquired or manufactured, is recorded when an item is sold. Higher inventory turnover can imply stronger sales relative to inventory levels whereas lower inventory turnover can imply slower sales or excess inventory. The faster a company sells its inventory, the quicker it can convert its assets to cash and improve liquidity. In addition, long inventory storage times can lead to obsolete inventory. Company X has the highest inventory turnover ratio of 4.3. (Choice B) Company Y has a lower inventory turnover ratio than Company X, meaning that Company Y was less efficient in converting its inventory into sales. (Choice C) Company Z has the lowest inventory turnover ratio.

question_en:
An analyst is evaluating several companies and has compiled the following information:

| ($ millions) | Credit Sales 20X1 | Accounts Receivable 20X1 | Credit Sales 20X2 | Accounts Receivable 20X2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Company 1 | 8.0 | 0.8 | 8.8 | 1.0 |
| Company 2 | 10.0 | 1.1 | 11.0 | 1.2 |
| Company 3 | 7.0 | 0.5 | 7.7 | 0.5 |

From 20X1 to 20X2, which company improved the most in days sales outstanding?
explanation_en: Days sales outstanding (DSO), sometimes referred to as days in receivables, calculates the number of days, on average, for a company to collect cash from its customers after sales are made on credit. It measures how quickly a company converts its receivables into cash. Faster collection of receivables results in a lower DSO, and this enhances a company's liquidity. By contrast, a higher DSO indicates that customers are too slow to pay invoices or that the company has poor credit extension policies (eg, not granting trade discount incentives for early payment), both of which can act as a drag on liquidity. It is helpful to gauge a company's DSO performance by comparing it across time, to that of the industry average, or to peers. Company 3 showed the most improvement from the previous year. It reduced its DSO by 2.4 days, meaning that it collected its receivables, on average, 2.4 days faster than it did for the previous year. (Choice A) Company 1 took 5.0 days longer, on average, to collect its receivables compared to its performance the prior year. (Choice B) Although Company 2 improved its DSO from the previous year (−0.3 days), the improvement was less than that of Company 3.

question_en:
A consultant is evaluating several companies and has collected the following information for the fiscal year:

| Company | Credit Sales ($ millions) | Cost of Goods Sold ($ millions) | Accounts Receivable Average Balance ($ millions) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 9.0 | 5.0 | 2.5 |
| 2 | 10.0 | 7.3 | 4.0 |
| 3 | 7.0 | 5.0 | 2.3 |

Which company has the best accounts receivable turnover?
explanation_en: The accounts receivable (AR) turnover ratio measures the number of times, on average, accounts receivable is generated by credit sales and collected as cash during a fiscal period. Credit sales occur when companies allow customers to defer sales invoice payments for a short period of time (commonly 30-60 days). Companies then record the amount owed from the customers as AR. A higher AR turnover ratio implies greater efficiency in converting receivables to cash and indicates better liquidity. This efficiency can result from a firm's effectiveness in receivables collection or from its credit-extension policies (eg, granting trade discount incentives for early payment). AR turnover for the three companies are as follows: Company 1 has the highest AR turnover ratio of 3.64, which means that it is the most efficient in collecting its AR among the three companies. (Choice B) Company 2 has collected on its AR 2.50 times on average during the year. This means that it was less efficient than Company 1 at converting receivables to cash. (Choice C) Company 3 has collected on its AR 3.04 times on average during the year. This means that it was less efficient that Company 1 at converting receivables to cash.

question_en: An analyst obtains the following information about a bond with no embedded options: If the bond's YTM increases by 1 basis point, the best estimate of the bond's price is closest to:
explanation_en:
A bond's money duration is its annual modified duration multiplied by the bond's full price. In this calculation, the full price is the bond's
market value, as none of the bonds have any accrued interest. Money duration is a measure of a bond's price sensitivity to a change in its YTM
expressed in the currency units of the bond's denomination.
Unlike other measures of price sensitivity (ie, modified and effective durations that estimate percentage price change, money duration estimates
the total change in value. Since it is weighted by the size of the position, money duration more effectively measures the impact individual bond
positions have on portfolio risk.
(Choice A) Bond X is the largest position by value invested but it has a much shorter duration than the other bonds.
(Choice C) Bond Z has the longest duration of the three bonds but has a much smaller weight in the portfolio than either of the other two
securities.

question_en:
An analyst has compiled the following data for a company:

| | Common Stock | Preferred Stock |
|---|---|---|
| Shares outstanding | 1,000,000 | 800,000 |
| Issue price | £20.00 | £25.00 |
| Current price | £47.60 | £28.00 |
| Dividend | £1.00 | £1.80 |
| Equity beta | 1.2 | — |
| Risk-free rate | 3% | — |
| Equity risk premium (ERP) | 5% | — |
| Tax rate | 20% | — |

The company recently issued £30 million in debt with a 6% yield. Assume that beta remains stable. Using the CAPM approach, which of the following is closest to the company's weighted average cost of capital (WACC)?
explanation_en:
The weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is a company's weighted average after-tax cost of capital from all sources. The most common sources of capital include equity, preferred stock, and debt. The WACC also represents the weighted average required return of all capital providers.

WACC = (wd)(rd)(1 - t) + (we)(re) + (wp)(rp)

For this question, use the steps below to calculate WACC using CAPM:

1. Determine current market values of capital (GBP millions): Debt: 30.00; Common: 1,000,000 x 47.60 = 47.60; Preferred: 800,000 x 28.0 = 22.40; Total: 100.00
2. Determine weight of each capital source: wd = 30%, we = 47.6%, wp = 22.4%
3. Recall given pre-tax cost of debt: rd = 6%
4. Use CAPM to determine cost of common equity: re = Rf + B(ERP) = 0.03 + 1.2(0.05) = 0.09
5. Determine the cost of preferred equity: rp = 1.80 / 28.00 = 0.0643
6. Input WACC variables:

WACC = (0.3)(0.06)(1 - 0.20) + (0.476)(0.09) + (0.224)(0.0643) = 7.16%

question_en:
A company receives cash of €55 million from the sale of equipment in 20X7. During that year, the company had depreciation expenses of €20 million and capital expenditures of €65 million; the capital expenditures were all used to purchase new equipment. The company reported the following balance sheet data:

| following balance sheet data: € millions | 20X7 | 20X6 |
|---|---|---|
| Gross cost of equipment | 800 | 760 |
| Accumulated depreciation | (150) | (140) |

Based on only this information, the gain on the sale of the equipment (in € millions) is closest to:
explanation_en: Cash flow treatment of investment income taxes paid US GAAP IFRS Investment CFO CFO or CFI income Income CFO, but can treat taxes paid CFO taxes on CFI income as CFI Cash flow statements divide cash inflows and outflows into three categories: cash from operations (CFO), cash from investing (CFI), and cash from financing (CFF). CFO encompasses cash inflows and outflows related to a company's daily activities. In contrast, CFI refers to inflows and outflows from noncore activities, such as passive investments in other companies. There are no income tax implications for CFF. In most cases, IFRS classify all taxes paid as CFO regardless of the underlying source of income. However, when a portion of the taxes can be specifically identified as paid on investment income, IFRS permit (but do not require) the company to classify that portion of the taxes as CFI. This company attributes €3 million of its total taxes paid to the rental income, which is not part of its core operations. The rents received constitute CFI, and the company may classify the taxes associated with those rents as CFI. The balance of the tax payment is classified as CFO. (Choices A and C) Financing activities that give rise to CFF entries include borrowing or repaying debt, issuing stock, and paying dividends. None of the taxes paid relate to any type of financing activity, so none can be classified as CFF.

subtopic: 5.04 Analyzing Statements of Cash Flows I
question_en:
A company reports the following information under US GAAP:

| Shareholders' equity item (USD millions) | Dec. 31, 20X1 | Dec. 31, 20X2 |
|---|---|---|
| Common stock | 200 | 205 |
| Additional paid-in capital | 500 | 570 |
| Accumulated other comprehensive income | 5 | 10 |
| Retained earnings | 300 | 345 |
| Total stockholders' equity | 1,005 | 1,130 |

In 20X2, all dividends declared were paid to shareholders. Based on only the data above, if net income for 20X2 is USD 55 million, 20X2 cash flow from financing activities (in USD millions) is closest to:
explanation_en:
A company's cash flows from financing activities relate to obtaining or repaying capital: issuing or repurchasing common stock, paying dividends, and borrowing or repaying debt. Here, net cash from financing activities includes the proceeds from issuing common stock (a cash inflow) and the payment of dividends (a cash outflow). The proceeds from issuing common stock equal the total change in common stock and additional paid-in capital. Dividends paid can be determined from the change in retained earnings, after accounting for net income.

Change in common stock = 205 - 200 = 5
Change in additional paid-in capital = 570 - 500 = 70
Dividends paid = Beginning retained earnings + Net income - Ending retained earnings = 300 + 55 - 345 = (10)

Cash flow from financing activities = 5 + 70 - 10 = 65.

(Choice A) 60 results from subtracting the increase in accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI), which mainly reflects unrealized gains/losses and is not an actual cash flow.
(Choice C) 85 results from incorrectly adding, instead of subtracting, dividends.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.09 Analysis of Income Taxes - Answers.pdf
question_en: A company reports the following information in its first year of operations: All else equal, if the tax rate had been 25% instead of 20%, then most likely the company's:
option_a: deferred tax assets would have been €750 lower.
option_b: deferred tax assets would have been €750 higher.
option_c: deferred tax liabilities would have been €750 higher.
explanation_en:
Deferred tax assets (DTA) and liabilities arise from temporary differences between income tax expense and taxes payable for a period. These
differences are expected to reverse over time and offset previous deferred tax items. Income tax expense is based on reported accounting
income from the income statement. Taxes payable is based on taxable income on the tax return and is the actual amount owed to the
government.
DTA arise when:
Taxable income > Accounting income and
Taxes payable > Tax expense.
Deferred tax liabilities (DTL) arise when:
Taxable income < Accounting income and
Taxes payable < Tax expense.
In this scenario, a DTA is created since taxable income is greater than accounting income (Choice C).
The deferred tax amount can be calculated as the product of the absolute difference between the taxable income and accounting income and the
tax rate. Therefore, the size of the deferred tax item is directly correlated to the tax rate. If the tax rate were higher, the amount of the DTA
increase would be higher as well (Choice A).

question_en: An analyst collects the following information (in € millions) on a company: Based on only this data, the company's income taxes payable (in € millions) is closest to:
explanation_en:
Deferred tax assets (DTAs) and liabilities (DTLs) reflect temporary differences between income tax expense and taxes payable, created by
differences between accounting standards and tax laws. Income tax expense is reported on the income statement according to accounting
standards, whereas taxes payable is the actual amount owed to the government based on applicable tax laws.
When tax expense is less than taxes payable, DTA is created since the company:
pays more in taxes in the current period and
will owe less in taxes in the future.
When tax expense is greater than taxes payable, DTL is created since the company:
pays less in taxes in the current period and
will owe more in taxes in the future.

question_en: An analyst gathers the following information about a company that reports under US GAAP: In Year 2, the decrease in net deferred tax assets most likely results from an increase in:
explanation_en:
Deferred tax assets (DTA) and liabilities (DTL) result from temporary differences between taxable income (based on tax reporting) and
accounting profit (based on financial reporting).
DTA are created when companies pay higher current taxes since taxable income is greater than accounting profit. This creates future tax
benefits, as in this scenario.
DTL are created when companies pay lower current taxes since taxable income is less than accounting profit. This creates future tax
liabilities.
The carrying amount of DTA represents the recoverable tax benefit, so if a company does not expect to generate enough taxable income to fully
recover the DTA, it must reduce the carrying amount. In that case, under US GAAP a company would create or increase a valuation allowance,
which is a contra account that decreases DTA. Under IFRS, the company reduces DTA directly and does not use a valuation allowance.
DTL and DTA (net of the valuation allowance) are combined and presented as net DTA (DTL) on the balance sheet. Therefore, an increase in the
valuation allowance would result in a decrease in the net DTA reported.
(Choice A) An increase in statutory tax rates would increase net DTA.
(Choice C) Since taxable income exceeds accounting profit in Year 2, there is an increase in DTA, not DTL.

question_en:
A company reports the following information:

```markdown
| (€ millions) | 20X8 | 20X7 |
|---|---|---|
| Deferred tax assets | 15 | 17 |
| Deferred tax liabilities | 29 | 24 |
| Tax expense | 19 | - |
```

Based on this information, the company's taxes payable for 20X8 are closest to:
explanation_en:
Tax expense appears on a company's income statement. It demonstrates what a company owes in taxes based on applicable accounting
standards. For some items, the tax laws mandate treatment different from accounting standards. This difference means that the taxes that the
company pays (or owes) are not the same as it reports as tax expense.
If the disparity between tax expense and taxes payable is expected to reverse in the future, the company creates a deferred tax asset (DTA) or a
deferred tax liability (DTL). A DTA signals investors that the company will pay less tax in the future than it pays in the current period; a DTL signals
the opposite.
Tax expense relates to taxes payable by adding the difference between the change in DTL and DTA for a given period. As a simple example, if a
company reports a tax expense of $20 and taxes payable of $12, it creates a DTL of $20 − 12 = $8 to account for the difference. If the company
had no previous DTL, its DTL increased by $8, and the above equality holds (ie, $20 = $12 + 8).
Rearrange the formula above to solve for taxes payable:
(Choice B) This choice incorrectly adds both the change in DTL and DTA.
(Choice C) This choice incorrectly adds the change in DTL and subtracts the change in DTA.
